summary:
Marsuit is a heads-up display on a Mars spacesuit's visor: a layered, hyperlocal map for a single Marswalk. It goes where tools like Mars Trek stop, down to each footstep. Our prototype runs on a phone placed inside a VR headset, and also offers a 3D simulation view.

The suit guides. On Curiosity's boxwork route on Mount Sharp, Marsuit layers data from three NASA missions. MRO's HiRISE height map, CRISM minerals and CTX images, Mars Odyssey's THEMIS thermal data, and Curiosity's RAD radiation, REMS weather and Navcam photos give six kinds of data. It plans the safest path around steep slopes, rough ground and real boulders, and replans when the astronaut changes route.

The suit thinks. Our MarStep equation prices every step in energy for a heavy suit: walking on loose ground, climbing, standing. It turns the cheapest way home into oxygen, and answers one question: can I still get home?

The suit talks. A voice agent explains "what's here?", and every stop shows Curiosity's own view and a science task.

A new way to use maps. You walk the real 3D terrain instead of reading it, and Ground Control follows live. When a solar storm hits, the suit sends you home before Earth even knows.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Marsuit is the display inside a Mars spacesuit's helmet for one surface walk. It turns the map into the place you walk through: the route, the dangers, the science and the "can I get home?" question are drawn right where you look. Our prototype runs on a phone placed inside a VR headset (or hand-held), with a 3D simulation view; the design is built for a real helmet visor.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Navigation on real terrain. We built a 3D model of Curiosity's 2025 boxwork route on Mount Sharp from the HiRISE 1 m height map (MRO). From it we compute slope and roughness, and find boulders in the HiRISE photo from their shadows. An A* planner finds the safest path, blocks ground over 20° (our team's safety limit) and replans every few seconds, or at once when the astronaut leaves the path.

2. MarStep, our energy equation. Power = standing cost + walking cost × ground factor + climbing cost against Mars gravity for a 180 kg astronaut-plus-suit. The ground factor comes from THEMIS thermal inertia (Mars Odyssey: loose vs. firm ground) and HiRISE roughness. A Dijkstra search finds the cheapest way home, energy is turned into oxygen (about 20.1 kJ per litre of O2), and the visor shows one score out of 100, the time to turn back and how much further you can go.

3. Layers. Zones on the ground show no-go slopes, careful slopes, rough ground, looser ground (THEMIS) and possible sulfates (CRISM). The 2D/3D Ground Control map adds CTX and Viking images of Gale crater.

4. Science stops. Each stop shows Curiosity's own Navcam photo of that spot, a task, the hazard and the science; a sample is logged by looking at the rock or taking a photo.

5. Safety and the Earth delay. Radiation (RAD), weather (REMS) and oxygen are watched all the time. In a solar storm or an oxygen leak the suit sends the astronaut home at once and speaks the warning; Ground Control gets it minutes later, because of the Earth–Mars light delay.

6. Voice. "Hey suit, what's here?" asks an AI voice agent about the spot, the minerals and the risks; every alert is also spoken.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Hyperlocal: it goes below the regional view of Mars Trek, to each step of one walk.

- Safety first: the path, the slope limit, the oxygen margin and the storm response all come from data, not guesses.

- A rehearsal tool: anyone can walk the real Mars terrain today, in a classroom or a park, and the same tool works for Artemis Moon walks with a different map.

TOOLS

JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), HTML canvas for the visor, three.js for the 3D terrain, Leaflet for the 2D map, PeerJS / a laptop link server for phone-to-laptop telemetry, Python + NumPy + Pillow to build the terrain, layers and boulders from NASA data, ElevenLabs for the voice agent and spoken alerts, Node's test runner (180+ tests), GitHub Pages for hosting.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Astronaut safety first; spacesuit mobility (suit mass, effort, loose ground); the Earth–Mars delay (the suit must act alone); being honest about data limits (THEMIS pixels are 100 m, CRISM 18 m, suit biosigns are simulated and labelled "simulated"); a calm display that only shows what the astronaut must decide on.
